Researchers investigated the effect of a novel antihypertensive agent, Hypertensol, on systolic blood pressure (SBP) in adults with stage 1 hypertension. A randomized, double‑blind, placebo‑controlled trial enrolled 200 participants who were assigned to one of five groups: placebo (n = 40), 10 mg (n = 40), 20 mg (n = 40), 40 mg (n = 40), or 80 mg (n = 40). After 12 weeks of daily dosing, mean SBP reductions (mmHg) and standard deviations (SD) were recorded. The investigators reported the following table of results:

| Dose (mg) | Mean SBP reduction (mmHg) | SD | n |
|-----------|---------------------------|----|---|
| 0 (Placebo) | 2.3 | 4.1 | 40 |
| 10 | 5.8 | 3.9 | 40 |
| 20 | 9.4 | 3.5 | 40 |
| 40 | 13.1 | 3.2 | 40 |
| 80 | 15.6 | 3.0 | 40 |

The authors concluded that Hypertensol produced a dose‑dependent reduction in SBP, with the 80‑mg dose yielding the greatest mean decrease. They also noted that the 80‑mg group had a p‑value < 0.001 compared to placebo, indicating a statistically significant difference.
stem: According to the table, which dose of Hypertensol produced the largest mean reduction in systolic blood pressure after 12 weeks?
explanation: The table shows the mean SBP reduction increases with dose; the 80‑mg group has the highest mean reduction of 15.6 mmHg.
trap: Choosing 40 mg because the curve flattens near the top, although 80 mg still has the highest mean (15.6 versus 13.1 mmHg).

trap: The presence of a placebo group might lead some to think it is a case‑control study, but the randomization and blinding are key distinguishing features.

stem: Which statement about the p-value (< 0.001) for the 80-mg group is correct?

options.A: The p‑value indicates the magnitude of the SBP reduction.
options.B: A p‑value < 0.001 means the result is clinically irrelevant.
options.C: If there were no true effect, a difference at least this large would be very unlikely to arise by chance.
options.D: A smaller p‑value always implies a larger sample size.

explanation: A p-value is the probability of data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true; it does not give effect size (A), does not imply clinical irrelevance (B), and does not depend monotonically on sample size alone (D).
trap: Treating the p-value as a measure of effect size or clinical importance.

stem: Which statement about the shape of the dose-response relationship is supported by Table 1?

options.A: Doubling from 40 mg to 80 mg added less reduction (2.5 mmHg) than doubling from 20 mg to 40 mg (3.7 mmHg)
options.B: Doubling from 40 mg to 80 mg added more reduction than doubling from 20 mg to 40 mg
options.C: The reduction rose by the same amount per mg at every dose
options.D: The 10 mg dose reduced SBP less than placebo

explanation: Correct: A) 15.6 − 13.1 = 2.5 mmHg for 40 to 80 mg, versus 13.1 − 9.4 = 3.7 mmHg for 20 to 40 mg, so the gain per doubling shrank at the top dose. Why the others are wrong: B) it reverses the actual increments (2.5 versus 3.7 mmHg). C) the gain per mg falls with dose, for example 0.35 mmHg/mg from 0 to 10 mg versus about 0.06 mmHg/mg from 40 to 80 mg. D) 10 mg lowered SBP by 5.8 mmHg versus 2.3 for placebo.
trap: Assuming more drug always gives proportionally more effect, ignoring that the increment from 40 to 80 mg is smaller than earlier ones.
